analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare Advantage plans to speed up and publish data on their prior authorization decisions.
analysis.headline: The House Ways and Means Committee approved the bill unanimously, 42–0, but it has not yet come to the full House or Senate floor.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Advantage plans are private insurers that cover about half of Medicare beneficiaries, and they can require doctors to get advance approval before providing care. This bill would require those plans to run a standardized electronic prior authorization system instead of fax machines and proprietary portals, publish detailed yearly data — including denial rates, appeal outcomes, response times, and how much they rely on artificial intelligence to make decisions — and meet basic standards to protect enrollees, with the option for the federal health agency to set firm deadlines for responses.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Advantage enrollees and their families, who would see faster approval decisions, clearer rules, and public data showing where plans delay or deny care. Doctors and hospitals also benefit from less paperwork and clearer criteria, and would be able to earn waivers from prior authorization if they follow the rules consistently.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Advantage plans that use prior authorization must establish a secure electronic program for submitting and answering requests, and fax machines, proprietary portals that fall short of federal standards, and simple electronic forms no longer count [S3].

Plans must report yearly to CMS — which must publish the data on a public website at the individual plan level — including the list of services requiring prior authorization, approval and denial rates, how often denied requests are overturned on appeal, average and median response times, and how often the plan used artificial intelligence or similar technology in its decisions [S3].

Enrollees can request access to the criteria a plan uses to make prior authorization decisions, and providers who contract with a plan get the criteria and an itemized list of required documentation [S3].

Plans must adopt enrollee protections, including transparent prior authorization programs developed with input from enrollees and providers, the ability to waive prior authorization for providers with strong compliance records, and annual reviews of which services require prior authorization [S3].

The bill gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to set response deadlines for prior authorization requests, such as 24 hours, including for expedited and real-time decisions, building on the existing 72-hour standard for expedited requests [S3].

CMS and the health information technology office must report by January 1, 2028 on how to move routinely approved services to real-time decisions and on how AI-driven decisions affect patient access, including for rural and low-income beneficiaries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers bear the cost of building electronic systems, collecting and reporting the required data, and meeting enrollee protection standards. If insurers pass those administrative costs on, it could show up in plan premiums or reduced plan extras. Taxpayers fund the government oversight, reporting, and rulemaking.

drawbacks.text: The bill regulates how quickly and transparently plans make prior authorization decisions but does not ban or limit the denials themselves, so a plan can still deny a service it has always denied [S3].
The response-time deadlines are discretionary: the Secretary 'may' establish timeframes rather than being required to, so the strength of the timeliness guarantee depends on future regulation [S3].

Compliance requires new reporting, technology, and annual reviews from every Medicare Advantage plan, administrative costs that insurers could pass on to beneficiaries through premiums or reduced supplemental benefits [S3].

Key benefits are back-loaded: transparency reporting begins with plan years starting on or after January 1, 2027, and the electronic program and enrollee protections begin with plan years starting on or after January 1, 2028, so patients may see no change for years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are real but modest: seniors get faster decisions and, for the first time, public plan-by-plan data on denials and appeals, which creates accountability even though the bill does not stop denials. The costs are mostly administrative and land on insurers, and the phased timeline means the biggest benefits arrive years after passage. On balance a worthwhile, incremental reform rather than a sweeping fix.

outcome.mechanism: The House Ways and Means Committee approved it unanimously in July 2026, but it has not yet been reported to the full House or considered by the Senate.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 20, 2025 by Rep. Mike Kelly (R-PA) with 73 original cosponsors from both parties, and quickly drew 304 total cosponsors (169 Democrats, 135 Republicans) [S1, S3, S4].
It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee (with the Health Subcommittee) and to Energy and Commerce [S5].
On June 25, 2026, the Health Subcommittee considered the bill and forwarded it to the full committee by voice vote [S5].
On July 15, 2026, the full Ways and Means Committee considered and ordered the bill reported in the nature of a substitute by a vote of 42–0 [S5].
The bill has not yet been reported to the House floor or received action in the Senate, and the 119th Congress is still in session [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost — the bill sits between committee approval and a floor vote. The insurance industry's interests are best served if it stalls here, since unanimous committee support makes defeat on the merits unlikely.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Up in the air between committee and floor

for.name: Rep. Mike Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in May 2025 and assembled a large bipartisan group of 73 original cosponsors across party lines.

for.name: 304 House cosponsors (169 Democrats, 135 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed onto the bill, giving it majority support in the House from both parties.

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Considered the bill on July 15, 2026 and ordered it reported in the nature of a substitute by a unanimous vote of 42–0.

against.name: Medicare Advantage insurance industry
against.role: Regulated insurers (via AHIP, the industry's trade association)
against.what_they_did: Has publicly opposed mandatory federal prior authorization requirements in this legislation across recent Congresses, arguing they add administrative burden and go beyond what plans have already adopted voluntarily.

sides.party_line_note: Support is heavily bipartisan: 304 cosponsors split 169 Democrats and 135 Republicans, the original cosponsor list spans both parties, and the Ways and Means Committee approved it 42–0 with no recorded opposition votes.

industries.note: The bill imposes compliance costs — electronic systems, annual data reporting, enrollee protections — and makes their denial rates, appeal outcomes, and use of AI publicly visible at the plan level, which the industry has opposed. Insurers benefit financially when prior authorization delays or deters costly care, so their interest in minimal restrictions runs against patients', even though faster electronic processing also saves them paperwork.

Providers get standardized electronic submissions instead of faxes and portals, clear written criteria and documentation requirements, and possible waivers from prior authorization if they comply consistently, reducing delays for their patients.

industries.industry: Health IT and electronic transaction vendors
industries.note: Every Medicare Advantage plan that uses prior authorization must build or buy systems meeting federal technical standards for electronic requests and responses, creating a large market for compliant software.

analysis.trajectory: With 304 cosponsors — more than a majority of the House — and a unanimous 42–0 committee vote, the bill is well positioned for House floor action, likely through a suspension-of-the-rules vote reserved for broadly supported bills, which requires a two-thirds majority. The bigger obstacle is the Senate, where the bill has no recorded action and needs its own path; prior versions of this legislation have died at exactly this stage despite broad support, and industry pressure to soften the mandatory reporting requirements is the main risk during any floor or Senate negotiation.
